notes:
I've written notes for every verse except 30–32. One limit up front: my search and fetch quota ran out before I reached netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. So the "Other views" points come only from what turned up incidentally, and I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage. The Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages cut off partway, so verses 41–47 depend more on the older commentaries.

**v. 25**
- Guzik's reading: using Caesar's coins meant accepting his civil authority, so the tax was owed. People bear God's image, so they belong to God, not to Caesar or even to themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Utley: the verb means paying back what is owed, so people do owe something to the government they live under. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- **Where Protestants differ:** Lutherans (LCMS) read the verse through Luther's "two kingdoms" teaching. Luther recognized, on the basis of Jesus' words… that there are two distinct realms. https://reporter.lcms.org/2016/president-harrison-provides-a-lutheran-view-of-church-and-state?amp=&amp=&amp= In this view a person's conscience and beliefs belong to God, not the state. The worldly kingdom is set up by God but runs by reason and natural law, not revelation. https://witness.lcms.org/2015/genius-and-courage/ The LCMS stresses that this doctrine does not require rigid separation of church and state. Neither institution should interfere with the unique responsibilities of the other. https://witness.lcms.org/2012/church-and-state-distinct-but-not-separate-4-2012/ Christians still have to disobey a government that takes over God's authority (Acts 5:29). https://reporter.lcms.org/2016/what-can-lutherans-do-as-voices-in-the-public-square An LCMS article contrasts this with views that a "Christian government" should impose biblical principles, naming the Puritans as an example. https://witness.lcms.org/2015/genius-and-courage/ GotQuestions (general evangelical) also says Jesus was separating two kingdoms: Caesar gets material things, Christ gets eternal ones. https://www.gotquestions.org/render-to-Caesar.html
- **Catholic/Orthodox (early church writers):** Aquinas's *Catena Aurea* on Mark's parallel collects several readings. Theophylact (an Orthodox archbishop): give the coin to the one whose image is on it. Bede: what belongs to God means tithes, firstfruits and offerings. Pseudo-Jerome: give yourselves to God, because God's light, not Caesar's, is stamped on us. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html

**v. 26**
- They later twisted this answer into a charge against him: in Luke 23:2 they claimed he forbade paying taxes to Caesar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Theophylact: men who should have believed only marvelled, because their trick had no room to work. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html

**v. 27**
- Guzik compares the Sadducees to modern liberal theologians: they rejected the supernatural, accepted only the five books of Moses, and denied immortality, spirits and angels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Matthew Henry: they denied not just the body's resurrection but any future life of the soul or reward and punishment. Remove that, he says, and all religion collapses. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm
- Utley: they were wealthy aristocrats who ran the high priesthood. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 28**
- The question is built on the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–10. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- Bridgeway: the brother was to have a temporary marriage with the widow to produce an heir. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-27.html

**v. 29**
- Spurgeon thought this was probably a stock story the Sadducees told to mock the resurrection. Stevenson compares it to "can God make a rock too heavy to lift?" https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- Bede thought something like it might really have happened. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html
- Pseudo-Jerome gives an allegory: the woman is the synagogue. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html

**v. 33**
- The Sadducees were arguing by *reductio ad absurdum*, trying to make resurrection look ridiculous. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- Henry: it doesn't matter whose wife she was, because death ends marriage and it is not resumed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**v. 34**
- Godet hears sarcasm in Jesus' answer: the piled-up marriage verbs cast contempt on a worldly outlook the Sadducees couldn't rise above. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsc/luke-20.html

**v. 35**
- Henry: "the resurrection" here means the blessed resurrection. The resurrection to condemnation is really a resurrection to death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/mhm/luke-20.html
- Utley: Jesus answers within Jewish (Pharisaic) theology. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-20.html
- Bock: the riddle falls apart because there is no marriage in the resurrection, and God is then the "parent." https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary

**v. 36**
- If no one dies, no one needs to be born, so marriage isn't needed. Jesus also quietly affirms that angels exist, which the Sadducees denied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Steven Cole: like the angels, we will not marry, die or sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- Theophylact: marriage exists now because we die; in the resurrection we will be unchanging, like angels. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html

**v. 37**
- Jesus proves the resurrection from the Torah alone, the only books the Sadducees accepted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Theophylact: Jesus says "I am," not "I was," and "Abraham" means the whole person, body and soul. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xii.html

**v. 38**
- Ellicott: only Luke adds "for all live to him." All true life depends on our relationship with God, and that relationship continues after death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-38.htm
- Gill: the patriarchs' souls live with God and their bodies will be raised. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-38.htm
- Alford: "I am thy God" implies a covenant, which could not be said of someone who had ceased to exist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-38.html
- **Differences in emphasis:** Calvin says believers who have died now live a heavenly life with God. Constable puts the weight on a future resurrection at the Second Coming. The Biblical Illustrator says the righteous dead are not asleep or unconscious. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-38.html
- **Scholarly note:** The Expositor's Greek Testament suggests "for all live unto Him" is probably an explanatory comment added by the writer, since it is not in the parallel Gospels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-38.htm
- A Lutheran sermon applies it this way: in Christ, all of you are alive. https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-2027-40-pentecost-22-series-c-2025

**v. 39**
- Utley: these scribes must have been Pharisees, glad to see the Sadducees beaten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-20.html
- Trapp: they praised Jesus because he had put down their rival party. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/luk-20.cfm

**v. 40**
- Utley: this covers both the Pharisees (vv. 19–26) and the Sadducees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-20.html
- Henry: his disciples, though weak, still dared to ask him questions; his critics no longer did. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**vv. 41–44**
- Henry: as God, Christ was David's Lord; as man, he was David's son. In Revelation's terms he is both David's "root" and David's "offspring." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm Coffman agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-20.html
- Utley (v. 42): the first "Lord" stands for God's personal name (YHWH), the second for *Adon* ("master"), meaning the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/luke-20.html
- Godet: Psalm 110 points directly to the Messiah, and calling himself David's Lord shows Jesus knew he was divine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsc/luke-20.html
- Chuck Smith (v. 44): no father would call his own son "Lord." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/luke-20.html

**v. 45**
- A Bible Hub sermon: Jesus warns publicly, not just to the guilty, because people were being taken in by these men. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/20-47.htm

**v. 46**
- Coffman calls these "embellishments of their vanity." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-47.html
- Henry's Concise: we should ask God to keep us from pride and ambition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-47.htm

**v. 47**
- Gill: verse 46 shows their pride, this verse their greed, covered by a show of devotion. Their guilt is greater than that of open sinners. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-47.html
- Barclay: rabbis were supposed to teach for free, but supporting a rabbi was praised as a great act of piety, which opened the door to exploiting widows. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/20-47.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that, according to Josephus, some Pharisees had great influence over women as spiritual advisers. https://biblehub.com/luke/20-47.htm
- The Cambridge Bible for Schools says "condemnation" really means "judgment," and theirs will be harsher than for people who kept none of these religious practices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-47.htm
- **Tone note:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown applies the verse to "the Romish clergy, the true successors of 'the scribes!'" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-47.htm
